title: Shavuot: a wedding at the mountain
hookLine: the rabbis picture Sinai as a wedding, the mountain held over the people like a canopy

lines: A CANOPY, A DOCUMENT, A PROMISE.
A MOUNTAIN IN SMOKE AND THUNDER.
WHAT IF IT WAS A WEDDING?
cards: At a Jewish wedding, the couple stands under a chuppah: a canopy, often just a prayer shawl or a cloth on four poles. A document is read, the ketubah, spelling out promises.

Words are spoken, something is given, and a crowd that was holding its breath bursts into song. Now a second scene: a mountain in cloud and smoke, thunder, a horn growing louder, a whole people gathered at its foot.
On Shavuot, Jews celebrate that day at Sinai. And the rabbis said what happened there was a wedding.

teach.b: Shavuot means weeks: the festival at the end of the seven weeks of counting. In the Torah it's a harvest feast, the first wheat; the rabbis tied it to the giving of the Torah at Sinai.
The wedding picture has old roots. The Mishnah, at the end of tractate Taanit, reads a verse from the Song of Songs about King Solomon's wedding day and says: that's the giving of the Torah.
On that reading, God is the groom and Israel the bride. The Torah's own description invites it.
In the old Jewish translation: "And Moses brought forth the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the nether part of the mount."
At the bottom of the mountain. But the Hebrew can also be read: underneath it. The Talmud, in Shabbat 88a, takes that literally, and the honest thing is to say the image isn't gentle.
God, it says, held the mountain over them like an overturned barrel: if you accept the Torah, good; if not, here will be your grave.

The Talmud itself is uneasy, and adds that the people later accepted it fully, freely, in the days of Esther. Some later teachers softened the picture: the mountain overhead became the wedding canopy.
And at its foot, the people's answer, in the old Jewish translation: "All that the LORD hath spoken we will do."
Some Sephardi communities read an actual marriage contract on Shavuot morning, a ketubah between God and Israel, a poem tradition credits to Israel Najara.
A promise made under a canopy of cloud.

how: On Shavuot, some Jews stay up through the night studying Torah, the Ten Commandments are read in the synagogue, and in some Sephardi communities a ketubah for Shavuot is read, portraying Sinai as the marriage of God and Israel.

games.q: you're at the foot of Sinai, and the Torah is offered. what does the Torah say the people answered?
o: all that the LORD hath spoken we will do.
games.why: all that the LORD hath spoken we will do: the answer at the foot of the mountain, like a vow.

practice: If you have a promise written down, wedding vows, a letter, a commitment you signed, read it slowly; if not, remember one, word for word if you can.
Ask yourself, without judgment: how is this promise doing, and what would it look like to make it again, freely, today?

wordCard.voice: Shavuot. Weeks: the festival at the end of the Omer, remembered as the day of Sinai, a wedding at the mountain. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: weeks, for the seven weeks counted from Passover.
